titre: Treated with Penicillin, Dead for Lack of Penicillin
accroche: In February 1941 in Oxford, penicillin pushes back a policeman's infection in a day; he relapses when the supply runs out, twelve years after the discovery
contenu_vulgarise:
In February 1941, at the Radcliffe Infirmary in Oxford, a policeman receives a penicillin infusion. Albert Alexander has a head covered in abscesses and has lost an eye; the treatments tried so far have changed nothing. Within twenty-four hours, his temperature drops, his appetite returns, the infection begins to heal. More than twelve years after the observation that revealed it, Albert Alexander is the first patient treated with penicillin injections. Yet there is not enough left to keep him alive.

## What Fleming Had Seen, and Had Not Done

In September 1928, on returning from vacation, Alexander Fleming finds a culture dish of staphylococci contaminated by a mold of the genus *Penicillium*: around it, the bacterial colonies have been destroyed. He publishes the observation in June 1929 in the *British Journal of Experimental Pathology*: the substance secreted by the mold inhibits several pathogenic bacteria. But the article attracts little attention. Fleming runs into the difficulty of producing it in large quantities and of isolating the active compound; even with the help of biochemists from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, chemical purification fails. In the 1930s, penicillin remains largely forgotten.

## What It Took to Make It a Drug

In Oxford, the biochemist Ernst Chain is working on lysozyme, an enzyme that destroys certain bacteria. Reading Fleming's articles in the *British Journal of Experimental Pathology*, he comes across the one devoted to *Penicillium* and, wrongly believing the substance to be an enzyme like lysozyme, judges it comparable. Chain and Howard Florey then decide to launch a major project on antibacterial substances produced by microorganisms. In September 1939, Florey asks the Medical Research Council for funds, which grants 250 pounds to start the project. A grant from the Rockefeller Foundation, of $5,000 a year for five years, is added later. Norman Heatley and Chain work out the extraction of penicillin by a solvent: Heatley devises a way to bring it back from the solvent into water by changing the acidity, and Chain proposes freeze-drying. The team obtains a dry brown powder, which it can test.

On May 25, 1940, Florey injects eight mice with a virulent strain of streptococcus and treats only four of them with penicillin. The next day, the four untreated are dead; the four treated are alive, although one of them dies two days later. The results, published in *The Lancet* on August 24, 1940, encourage the team to move on to humans. But Florey reminds his collaborators that a man weighs three thousand times more than a mouse: producing enough penicillin for an adult remains an obstacle.

## A Body That Recycles What Is Missing

On February 12, 1941, Alexander receives an infusion of 160 mg of penicillin, or 200 units. The improvement is clear, but the team has extracted only a small quantity of penicillin: it recovers what is excreted in his urine to give it back to him. By the fifth day, there is none left. Alexander relapses and dies on March 15, 1941. Florey and his team then decide to treat only young children, who do not need such strong doses, until their production methods improve.

What this delay of more than twelve years reveals is that spotting a biological effect and turning it into a treatment are not the same operation. Fleming had been right; but purifying an unstable molecule, producing it in quantity, and calculating a human dose required another team and another budget. Florey said it himself: his team was not thinking of suffering humanity, but of an interesting scientific exercise. The shortage that kills Alexander is not an accident of history: it is the distance between discovering a promising molecule and knowing how to manufacture it in quantity.

repere.texte: On May 25, 1940, Florey infects eight mice with a virulent strain of streptococcus and treats only four of them with penicillin: the next day, the four untreated are dead, the four treated are alive.
repere.source: Wikipedia, article “Howard Florey,” section on the development of penicillin

carte.punch: Improved in a day by penicillin, dead a month later for lack of penicillin.
carte.idee: In February 1941, the policeman Albert Alexander becomes the first patient treated with penicillin injections: his temperature drops within 24 hours. But more than twelve years after Fleming's discovery, production is still not enough, and he relapses and then dies for lack of supply.

quiz.question: Why does Albert Alexander's treatment stop after five days, even though his condition was improving?
choix: Because the doctors judge him cured and stop the treatment
Because penicillin proves toxic at high doses in adults
Because the laboratory's supply of penicillin, recycled from his urine, runs out
Because Alexander refuses to continue the treatment for fear of side effects
quiz.explication: Penicillin was so scarce in 1941 that the team recovered what was excreted in the patient's urine to give it back to him; by the fifth day, none was left, neither to produce nor to recycle. The sources attribute the stoppage to this shortage, not to toxicity or to a refusal by the patient.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Ernst Chain come to take an interest in penicillin?
choix: An article by Pasteur on the fermentation of molds puts him on the trail
While working on lysozyme, he reads Fleming's articles in the British Journal of Experimental Pathology and comes across the one devoted to Penicillium
An experiment run independently by Howard Florey on mice convinces him
The Nobel Prize awarded to Fleming in 1938 draws Oxford's attention to the mold
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Chain was working on lysozyme. Reading Fleming's articles in the British Journal of Experimental Pathology, he comes across the one devoted to Penicillium, and the mistaken impression that the substance is an enzyme like lysozyme leads him to take an interest in it. The mouse experiment dates from 1940, and Fleming received the Nobel only in 1945.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the May 25, 1940, experiment on the eight mice show?
choix: All eight infected mice survive thanks to a vaccine
The next day, the four mice treated with penicillin are alive and the four untreated are dead
Penicillin kills the mice as fast as the infection itself
No mouse survives, which delays the project by two years
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Florey infects eight mice with a virulent strain of streptococcus and treats only four of them with penicillin: the next day, the four untreated are dead, the four treated are alive (one of them dies two days later).

quiz_supplementaire.question: After Albert Alexander's death, toward whom does Florey redirect his clinical trials?
choix: Toward young children, who require lower doses
Toward healthy volunteers to test toxicity
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Children require lower doses: the team could continue the trials with the little penicillin available, until its production methods improved.
